summary: The deck explains frugal services as low-cost, reliable, and accessible service models that maximize value through efficient resource use, and discusses why they are harder to assess than frugal products because they require end-to-end process and reliability analysis. It presents a three-heuristic framework for frugal service innovation—bricolage, reducing time/materials/human effort, and creating self-service options—illustrated with case studies including SuperSeva, Mumbai Dabbawalas, Indian software firms, Jayashree Industries, missed-call services, and Vortex-Gramateller ATMs.

content: Heuristics of Frugal Service Innovations, 2014 Proceedings of PICMET '14
Frugal innovation is not limited to physical products. It can also be applied to services.
Frugal services are cost-effective, reliable, and accessible service solutions designed to deliver maximum value by minimizing the use of resources without compromising service quality.
Deliver high-quality services at the lowest possible cost through innovative service design and efficient resource utilization.
Requirement for reliable and error-free services
Need to serve large customer at affordable prices
Importance of scalable and sustainable service models
Objective:Develop services that reduce operational cost while maintaining reliability.
Why are frugal services harder to identify than frugal products?
A physical product can often be examined directly.
For example, an expert can look at a device and evaluate whether it uses fewer components, uses low-	cost materials, simpler design, or provides good performance at a low price.
However, a service is different because its cost and quality depend on many connected processes.
To evaluate whether a service is truly frugal, we need to examine the complete service process:
Input → People → Resources → Process → Service delivery → Outcome
We must also check whether the service remains reliable over time.
Service innovation requires detailed process mapping and analysis of reliability.
Reducing Time, Materials and Human Effort
Use existing infrastructure, materials, and processes instead of creating new ones.
Utilize existing government and commercial services
Used railway network, bicycles, and hand carts
Extremely low delivery cost with high accuracy
Heuristic 2 – Reducing Time, Materials & Human Effort
Traditional self-service systems from developed countries may not always work directly in developing countries.
Higher-income customers may prefer personal assistance.
Lower-income users may find complicated self-service technologies difficult to use.
Innovators must design self-service options that are simple, familiar, affordable, easy to understand, and suitable for local users.
A company advertises a specific phone number.
A customer gives a missed call to that number.
The call is not answered, so the customer is not charged.
The automated system recognizes the call.
The customer receives the required information or service automatically.
The example shows how self-service can be redesigned for remote and resource-constrained areas.
suitable for areas with unreliable electricity
accessible to users with limited literacy.
Summary: Three simple innovation principles (heuristics) for creating low-cost but reliable services, especially for developing countries where customers are highly price-sensitive.
